nouns.articleHelp: Short/monosyllabic noun — no suffix or semantic rule applies. Short neuter nouns are less common (~25% of monosyllables). Many short das-nouns form -er plurals (Buch→Bücher, Kind→Kinder, Haus→Häuser). Memorize in context.
nouns.pluralHelp: -e (die Jahre). Rule: Some neuter nouns take -e, usually WITHOUT umlaut: Jahr→Jahre, Spiel→Spiele, Ziel→Ziele, Tier→Tiere. Neuter -e plurals rarely umlaut (exception: das Floß→Flöße).

nouns.articleHelp: Semantic note: das Kind — neuter despite referring to a person. This is a famous case where grammatical gender ≠ natural gender. Same for das Baby, das Mädchen (-chen diminutive → always das).
nouns.pluralHelp: -er (die Kinder). Rule: The -er plural is the signature neuter pattern for short nouns. E.g. Kind→Kinder, Buch→Bücher, Haus→Häuser, Bild→Bilder. Almost always adds umlaut if possible.

nouns.articleHelp: ⚠ Weak noun (n-Deklination): This noun takes -(e)n in ALL cases except nominative singular. den Menschen, dem Menschen, des Menschen. Recognizing weak nouns is crucial for correct case usage beyond just the article.
nouns.pluralHelp: -(e)n (die Menschen). ⚠ Weak noun (n-Deklination): This noun takes -(e)n not just in plural, but in ALL cases except nominative singular. den Menschen, dem Menschen, des Menschen. The plural form is the same as the accusative/dative/genitive singular. Weak nouns must be memorized as a group.

nouns.articleHelp: Morphological: Nominalized infinitive → always das. Any German verb can be used as a noun (capitalize it), and it's always neuter. das Leben (to live → life), das Essen (to eat → food).
nouns.pluralHelp: No change (die Unternehmen). Rule: Masculine and neuter nouns ending in -er, -el, -en usually keep the same plural form. Some add an umlaut (Vater→Väter), but many don't (Fenster→Fenster). The article change to 'die' is your only plural signal.

nouns.articleHelp: Short/monosyllabic noun — no suffix or semantic rule applies. Short feminine nouns are the rarest monosyllables (~15%). Many form plurals with umlaut + -e (Hand→Hände, Nacht→Nächte, Stadt→Städte).
nouns.pluralHelp: -(e)n (die Zeiten). Rule: The most common feminine plural. Nearly all die-nouns that don't end in -e take -(e)n: Frau→Frauen, Tür→Türen, Uhr→Uhren, Zahl→Zahlen. When you know it's die, guess -(e)n for the plural and you'll usually be right.

nouns.articleHelp: Short/monosyllabic noun — no suffix or semantic rule applies. Statistically, ~60% of monosyllabic German nouns are der, ~25% das, ~15% die. But that's a gamble, not a rule. Best memorized in a phrase: 'der Hund bellt', 'der Weg ist lang'.
nouns.pluralHelp: -e (die Tage). Rule: The default masculine plural. Monosyllabic der-nouns very often take -e, frequently with umlaut: Tag→Tage, Stuhl→Stühle, Kopf→Köpfe, Hund→Hunde. Tip: if it's der and one syllable, try -e (±umlaut) first.

nouns.articleHelp: Greek/Latin origin ending in -ma → das. Das Thema, das Drama, das Klima, das Dogma, das Trauma. Very reliable neuter pattern.

nouns.articleHelp: No standard suffix or semantic rule applies cleanly. Masculine gender must be memorized. Tip: ~60% of monosyllabic German nouns are der, but "Euro" has 2 syllables — memorize with a phrase.
nouns.pluralHelp: No change (die Euro). Rule: In counting/financial contexts, "Euro" stays unchanged: "5 Euro". Colloquially "Euros" exists but the official plural is invariant. Similar to "100 Prozent".

nouns.articleHelp: Short/monosyllabic noun — no suffix or semantic rule applies. Short feminine nouns are the rarest monosyllables (~15%). Many form plurals with umlaut + -e (Hand→Hände, Nacht→Nächte, Stadt→Städte).
nouns.pluralHelp: -e + umlaut (die Städte). Feminine nouns with -e plural are less common but important — they almost always take umlaut: Hand→Hände, Nacht→Nächte, Kraft→Kräfte, Stadt→Städte, Wand→Wände, Angst→Ängste. These are mostly monosyllabic. The umlaut shifts the stem vowel (a→ä, o→ö, u→ü) — this is common in monosyllabic masculine and feminine nouns.

nouns.articleHelp: Adjectival noun (substantivized adjective). With definite article it takes weak endings: der Jugendliche, die Jugendliche, des Jugendlichen, dem Jugendlichen, den Jugendlichen. Without article (strong): ein Jugendlicher.
nouns.pluralHelp: die Jugendlichen (with article — weak adj. ending). Without article: "Jugendliche" (strong adj. ending). Adjectival nouns are declined like their corresponding adjectives.

Feminine nouns with -e plural are less common but important — they almost always take umlaut: Hand→Hände, Nacht→Nächte, Kraft→Kräfte, Stadt→Städte, Wand→Wände, Angst→Ängste. These are mostly monosyllabic. The umlaut shifts the stem vowel (a→ä, o→ö, u→ü) — this is common in monosyllabic masculine and feminine nouns.

nouns.articleHelp: Semantic note: Body parts have no reliable gender rule — they're spread across all three genders. der Kopf, die Nase, das Auge. Each must be memorized individually.
nouns.pluralHelp: -e + umlaut (die Zähne). Rule: The default masculine plural. Monosyllabic der-nouns very often take -e, frequently with umlaut: Tag→Tage, Stuhl→Stühle, Kopf→Köpfe, Hund→Hunde. Tip: if it's der and one syllable, try -e (±umlaut) first. The umlaut shifts the stem vowel (a→ä, o→ö, u→ü) — this is common in monosyllabic masculine and feminine nouns.

nouns.articleHelp: Pattern: -er ending → usually der. Covers agents, tools, instruments, and many other categories. But beware: das Fenster, das Wasser, das Messer, das Feuer, das Zimmer are common neuter exceptions.
nouns.pluralHelp: No change (die Zucker). Rule: Masculine and neuter nouns ending in -er, -el, -en usually keep the same plural form. Some add an umlaut (Vater→Väter), but many don't (Fenster→Fenster). The article change to 'die' is your only plural signal.

nouns.articleHelp: Suffix pattern: Stressed -ie → usually die (French/Latin origin). E.g. Energie, Philosophie, Therapie, Industrie.

nouns.articleHelp: Pattern: -er ending → usually der. Covers agents, tools, instruments, and many other categories. But beware: das Fenster, das Wasser, das Messer, das Feuer, das Zimmer are common neuter exceptions.
nouns.pluralHelp: No change (die Panzer). Rule: Masculine and neuter nouns ending in -er, -el, -en usually keep the same plural form. Some add an umlaut (Vater→Väter), but many don't (Fenster→Fenster). The article change to 'die' is your only plural signal.

nouns.articleHelp: Ending pattern: ~90% of nouns ending in -e are die. This is one of the strongest gender-guessing heuristics in German. When in doubt on an -e noun, guess die.
nouns.pluralHelp: +n (die Pleiten). Rule: Nouns ending in -e simply add -n. Extremely consistent for feminine nouns (Straße→Straßen, Lampe→Lampen, Schule→Schulen). Also applies to masculine weak nouns ending in -e (Kollege→Kollegen, Löwe→Löwen).

nouns.articleHelp: Adjectival noun (substantivized adjective). With the definite article it takes weak adjective endings: der/die Übergewichtige (sg.), die Übergewichtigen (pl.). Without article (strong endings): ein Übergewichtiger, Übergewichtige (pl.).

nouns.articleHelp: No standard suffix, semantic, or morphological rule applies cleanly. Neuter gender must be memorized. Tip: learn it as a chunk — 'das Ziel erreichen', not just 'das Ziel'.
nouns.pluralHelp: -er + umlaut (die Vorblätter). Rule: The -er plural with umlaut is a signature neuter pattern. E.g. Buch→Bücher, Haus→Häuser, Wald→Wälder. Almost exclusive to das-nouns, with a few der-exceptions (Mann→Männer).

nouns.articleHelp: Compound noun — gender follows the last element: Bein (das). This is the #1 rule in German: always look at the final component.
nouns.pluralHelp: -e (die Vorderbeine). Rule: Some neuter nouns take -e, usually WITHOUT umlaut: Jahr→Jahre, Spiel→Spiele, Ziel→Ziele, Tier→Tiere. Neuter -e plurals rarely umlaut (exception: das Floß→Flöße).

nouns.articleHelp: Compound noun — gender follows the last element: Haus (das). This is the #1 rule in German: always look at the final component.
nouns.pluralHelp: -er + umlaut (die Vorderhäuser). Rule: The -er plural with umlaut is a signature neuter pattern. E.g. Buch→Bücher, Haus→Häuser, Wald→Wälder. Almost exclusive to das-nouns, with a few der-exceptions (Mann→Männer).

nouns.articleHelp: ⚠ Weak noun (n-Deklination): This noun takes -(e)n in ALL cases except nominative singular. den Menschen, dem Menschen, des Menschen. Recognizing weak nouns is crucial for correct case usage beyond just the article.
nouns.pluralHelp: -(e)n (die Vorfahren). Some masculine nouns take -(e)n plural, especially weak nouns (n-Deklination). E.g. Mensch→Menschen, Staat→Staaten, Typ→Typen.

nouns.articleHelp: Compound noun — gender follows the last element: Halle (die). This is the #1 rule in German: always look at the final component.
nouns.pluralHelp: +n (die Vorhallen). Rule: Nouns ending in -e simply add -n. Extremely consistent for feminine nouns (Straße→Straßen, Lampe→Lampen, Schule→Schulen). Also applies to masculine weak nouns ending in -e (Kollege→Kollegen, Löwe→Löwen).

nouns.articleHelp: Compound noun — gender follows the last element: Kampf (der). This is the #1 rule in German: always look at the final component.
nouns.pluralHelp: -e + umlaut (die Vorkämpfe). Rule: Many masculine monosyllabic nouns take -e with umlaut: Stuhl→Stühle, Kopf→Köpfe, Arzt→Ärzte, Sohn→Söhne. One of the most common masculine plural patterns.

nouns.articleHelp: Compound noun — gender follows the last element: Kammer (die). This is the #1 rule in German: always look at the final component.
nouns.pluralHelp: die Vorratskammern. Irregular or mixed plural pattern. Best memorized directly.

nouns.articleHelp: Compound noun — gender follows the last element: Redner (der). This is the #1 rule in German: always look at the final component.
nouns.pluralHelp: No change (die Vorredner). Rule: Masculine and neuter nouns ending in -er, -el, -en usually keep the same plural form. Some add an umlaut (Vater→Väter), but many don't (Fenster→Fenster). The article change to 'die' is your only plural signal.

nouns.articleHelp: Compound noun — gender follows the last element: Spann (der). This is the #1 rule in German: always look at the final component.
nouns.pluralHelp: -e (die Vorspanne). Rule: The default masculine plural. Monosyllabic der-nouns very often take -e, frequently with umlaut: Tag→Tage, Stuhl→Stühle, Kopf→Köpfe, Hund→Hunde. Tip: if it's der and one syllable, try -e (±umlaut) first.
